title: Charges between City departments, year by year
question: How much do City departments charge one another each year, is the share growing, and what has the Board’s analyst found about how those charges are managed?
finding: Departments charged one another $1.34 billion in fiscal 2026, against $909.7 million in fiscal 2019 (47% more). Day-to-day spending rose 46% over the same years, so the share barely moved: 7.6% then, 7.7% now, and between 7.0% and 8.9% in every year since fiscal 1999 that the ledger records in full. Nothing unusual in the total. What the Board’s analyst found in April 2025 was about management: “appropriations for interdepartmental services had between $53 and $80 million across all funds remaining at year-end”; of 48 charges sampled, “departments only provided MOUs for half”; and “At least two interdepartmental service agreements in our sample had hourly rates that exceeded at least some private-sector rates for similar services”.
how: The Controller’s Spending and Revenue table, fiscal 1999 to 2026. Internal charges are spending lines of the kind “Services Of Other Depts”; recoveries are the matching revenue lines of the kind “Expenditure Recovery” in the departments that did the work. Day-to-day spending adds salaries, benefits, purchased services, supplies, grants and aid, and the internal charges themselves, and leaves out capital, debt, pension payments and transfers between funds. Fiscal 2018 is shown for the charges only: in that year the source files most purchased services under a different heading and records only part of the recoveries, so its totals are not comparable. The quotations are from the Budget and Legislative Analyst’s performance audit of 28 April 2025.
limits: Charging between departments is ordinary: the ledger’s own lines are for power bought from the utility, legal services from the City Attorney, rent paid to the Real Estate Division and repairs at the central shops. The audit quoted here found weak paperwork and money budgeted but not spent, not money missing; it records the Controller agreeing with thirteen of the fourteen recommendations made to it, and the Mayor’s budget office with four of eight and partly with the other four. An internal charge is in the ledger twice, as the buyer’s spending and as the seller’s recovery, so adding departments’ budgets together counts the same work twice. The audit says departments “lack sufficient visibility into actual spending on interdepartmental services (IDS) due to a software functionality issue”, so a charge cannot be followed to a unit of work from public data. What would settle whether a given charge is fair: the memorandum of understanding for it, with the unit cost and the bills.

sources.t: San Francisco Controller: Spending and Revenue, by department, account and fiscal year (DataSF)
